title: Trump Threatens to Destroy Iranian Infrastructure as US-Iran War Escalates
excerpt: The U.S. president vowed to bomb a bridge or power plant for every Iranian attack on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, prompting Tehran to warn it would target regional energy facilities and block all oil exports.
body:
• Trump threatens to bomb Iranian infrastructure in response to attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
  • Iran warns it will retaliate by targeting regional energy facilities if the U.S. follows through on its threats.
  • Houthi threats to block Saudi oil exports have driven Brent crude prices above $94 a barrel.
  • The ongoing conflict has resulted in 18 U.S. service member deaths and over 450 injuries since June, while Iran reports 53 civilian deaths and 592 injuries.
Key Takeaways
  • Trump threatens to bomb Iranian infrastructure for every attack on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
  • Iran warns it will retaliate by targeting regional energy facilities if attacked.
  • Houthi threats to block Saudi oil exports have pushed Brent crude prices above $94 a barrel.
  • The conflict has resulted in 18 U.S. service member deaths and over 450 injuries since June.
  • Iran reports 53 civilian deaths and 592 injuries amid ongoing military actions.

A New Red Line in the Strait of Hormuz

President Donald Trump drew a sharp new red line against Iran on Wednesday, declaring that the United States would destroy a bridge or power plant — including those "in the Capital City of Tehran" — every time Iranian forces fire on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.

"From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The escalation came on the 11th straight night of U.S. bombing inside Iran and as the broader conflict, launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, continues to expand in scope and intensity.

Tehran Fires Back With Economic Threats

Iran responded within hours. Its joint military command warned, according to state media, that Iranian forces would target regional oil, gas, electricity and economic infrastructure and prevent the export of "even a single drop of oil" if Trump carried out his threat.

"Our defense doctrine is clear: eye for an eye. Any aggression against Iran, including our infrastructure, will compel a powerful and decisive response. Those who contribute to such aggression, whatever the kind of support, will also be considered as legitimate targets."

— Abbas Araqchi, Iranian Foreign Minister

An anonymous military source linked to the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim News went further, stating that if Americans attack any bridge or power station, Iran would strike "infrastructure and bridges in the region, including energy facilities where the United States has interests."

A Second Chokepoint Under Threat

The standoff deepened as Iranian-allied Houthis in Yemen threatened to block Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a move that would put a second vital energy route at risk. Five tankers changed course in the Red Sea on Wednesday to avoid the strait, according to Reuters. Three tankers loaded with Saudi oil bound for China and India had already made U-turns the day before.

Millions of barrels of Saudi crude had been rerouted to the kingdom's Red Sea port of Yanbu to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. If the Bab el-Mandeb is also blocked, shipments would be forced through the Suez Canal, adding weeks to journeys and raising freight costs significantly.

Brent crude futures hit more than $95 a barrel before settling just above $94. U.S. gasoline prices have climbed back over $4 a gallon, weighing on Trump's approval ratings ahead of November's midterm elections.

Mounting Human and Economic Costs

Trump traveled to Dover Air Force Base on Wednesday for the arrival of the remains of four U.S. service members killed in Iranian attacks on military bases — three in Jordan and one in Iraq. The war has now claimed 18 American lives and injured more than 450 troops. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told a Senate hearing that the U.S. had spent $37.5 billion on the conflict so far.

An Iranian health ministry official said 53 civilians had been killed and 592 wounded since late last month. Iran's power grid has already lost 4,200 megawatts of capacity from recent strikes, with 2,000 MW in direct damage, according to Tavanir CEO Mohammad Allah-Dad.

Iran pounded vital water desalination and energy plants in Kuwait this week and targeted U.S. military assets in Bahrain and Jordan. Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain all reported intercepting Iranian attacks.

Ceasefire Talks Hanging by a Thread

Mediators have presented Iran with a proposal for a 10-day ceasefire aimed at salvaging an interim agreement signed in June. Pakistan's foreign ministry said it would continue its mediating efforts but insisted shipping safety must be assured.

"Tehran is trying to create leverage for a negotiation."

— Mahmoud Shehrah, Associate Fellow, Chatham House

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that allowing Iran to control the strait would set a dangerous precedent, including in the South China Sea. "If they're serious, we're serious. If they're not, then we will do what's necessary to protect our interests, and also the interests of our allies," he told reporters in Manila.

Iran has insisted on maintaining the control over the Strait of Hormuz it established during the war. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf appeared to brush off Trump's threat, stating that "the situation of the strait will not return to prewar conditions."

What to Watch

For Indian energy consumers, the dual threat to Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb is particularly concerning. India imports roughly 85% of its crude oil, with a significant share transiting these waterways. Any sustained disruption could push already elevated fuel prices higher and widen the current account deficit. The coming days will test whether diplomatic channels can prevent the conflict from spiraling into a full-scale regional energy crisis.
